name: Agent harnesses
examples: SWE-bench style eval runs in Docker sandboxes
summary: The scaffolding that turns an LLM into an agent: a loop that calls the model, executes the tools it requests, feeds results back, and manages context, sandboxing, limits and stopping.
why: Agent quality depends heavily on the harness (tools, context, limits), and the same harnesses drive agent evals and RL rollout environments.
keyIdeas: Loop: model call, run tool calls, append results, repeat until a final text answer with no tool calls
Stopping and control: max turns or budget caps (MaxTurnsExceeded, error_max_turns), plus human checkpoints
Context management: auto compaction summarizes older history near the window limit, keeping recent turns
Agent-computer interface (SWE-agent): tool design and docs strongly affect agent performance

name: SGLang
examples: Structured outputs via XGrammar, Outlines or llguidance
Overlap scheduler (CPU scheduling overlapped with GPU)
Rollout engine in verl, slime, AReaL, Miles
summary: Open-source inference framework from sgl-project (hosted by LMSYS) for LLMs, VLMs and diffusion models, aimed at agentic workloads, large-scale serving and RL rollouts.
why: Widely used both as a production serving engine and as the rollout generator inside RL post-training frameworks.
keyIdeas: RadixAttention keeps KV cache in a radix tree for automatic prefix reuse; eviction policies include lru and lfu
Paper adds compressed finite state machines for faster constrained decoding; XGrammar is the default grammar backend
Many attention backends (FlashInfer, FA3/FA4, Triton, FlashMLA, TRTLLM MLA, AITER), auto-selected per hardware
Runs on NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Intel, Apple Silicon, Huawei Ascend and Moore Threads hardware

name: KV cache offloading
examples: vLLM OffloadingConnector (CPU tier plus optional FS, object-store or P2P tiers)
SGLang HiCache (GPU L1, host L2, storage L3)
NixlConnector / MooncakeConnector for prefill-to-decode KV transfer
summary: Moving KV cache out of GPU HBM into CPU memory, local disk or remote storage so it can be reused across requests, sessions and engine instances instead of being recomputed by prefill.
why: Prefix-cache hits are capped by HBM size; offload tiers turn repeated long contexts (multi-turn, agents, RAG) into KV loads instead of prefill, cutting TTFT.
keyIdeas: Extends prefix caching: vLLM copies completed blocks to pinned host memory with async DMA and promotes hits back to GPU on demand
SGLang HiCache: HiRadixTree over GPU (L1), instance-private host (L2), shared storage L3 (Mooncake, 3FS, NIXL, file)
Load vs recompute: HiCache prefetch policies (best_effort, wait_complete, timeout) and vLLM max_load_tokens bound transfer time
The same KV connector API ships KV from prefill to decode workers in disaggregated serving (LMCache, NIXL, Mooncake)

name: vLLM attention backends
summary: vLLM's pluggable attention kernels (AttentionBackendEnum), chosen with --attention-backend or --attention-config.backend; by default vLLM picks the first backend in a priority list that validates for the model and GPU.
why: The backend decides which KV dtypes, block sizes, head sizes and GPUs work, so it directly drives latency and whether a model config runs at all.
keyIdeas: Auto-selection walks a priority list, validating dtype, KV dtype, block size, head size and compute capability
FlashAttention defaults to FA4 on SM100+, FA3 on SM90, FA2 otherwise; override with flash_attn_version
MLA uses separate backends: decode via -ac.backend (FLASHMLA, TRITON_MLA), prefill via -ac.mla_prefill_backend
Backends differ on FP8 KV cache, attention sinks, sparse MLA, non-causal and DCP; ROCm and CPU use their own

name: FlashInfer
examples: Paged and ragged KV-cache attention (decode, prefill, append)
FP8/FP4 GEMM and fused MoE kernels
summary: A kernel library and generator for LLM inference with unified APIs for attention, GEMM, MoE, sampling and communication, backed by its own kernels plus FlashAttention-2/3, cuDNN, CUTLASS and TensorRT-LLM.
why: It is a kernel layer under engines like vLLM and SGLang, so its paged-KV formats and attention variants shape what those engines can serve fast.
keyIdeas: Handles heterogeneous KV-cache storage with block-sparse and composable formats to cut redundant memory access
Customizable attention template compiled JIT; optional prebuilt cubin and jit-cache wheels skip first-use compiles
Load-balanced scheduling adapts to dynamic batches while staying CUDAGraph compatible
README lists SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI and MLC-LLM among adopters

name: CUTLASS and CuTe
examples: CUTLASS C++ GEMM templates (FP64 down to NVFP4/MXFP4)
summary: NVIDIA CUTLASS is a CUDA C++ template library for high-performance GEMM and related kernels; CuTe (since CUTLASS 3.0) adds Layout and Tensor abstractions, and CUTLASS 4 adds the Python CuTe DSL.
why: FlashAttention-3/4, FlashInfer backends and vLLM's CUTLASS_MLA build on it to reach Tensor Core peak on Hopper and Blackwell.
keyIdeas: GEMM decomposed hierarchically into reusable tiling, data-movement and MMA pieces tuned by tile size, dtype and policy
CuTe layouts are hierarchical multidimensional maps, combined by functional composition to build tiling and partitioning
CuTe DSL exposes the same layouts, tensors and hardware atoms from Python with much faster compile times
FlashAttention-3 uses CUTLASS abstractions on Hopper; FlashAttention-4 is written in CuTe DSL for Hopper and Blackwell

name: Knowledge distillation (teacher to student)
examples: Ensemble compression into one deployable model
summary: Training a smaller student model to match the output distribution (soft targets) of a larger teacher or ensemble, instead of only the hard labels, so most of the teacher's quality fits in a cheaper model.
why: Lets you serve a smaller, faster model (lower latency and cost) that keeps much of a large model's quality, a common step before deployment.
keyIdeas: Soft targets: use the teacher's class probabilities as training targets; they carry more information than one-hot labels
Temperature: raise the softmax temperature for teacher and student so small probabilities still give signal
Hinton et al. scale soft-target gradients by T squared when mixing with the hard-label loss
DistilBERT: 40% smaller, 60% faster, keeps 97% of BERT's language understanding (per its paper)

name: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
summary: Learning rankers from clicks while correcting for presentation bias: a click model estimates how likely each position is examined (the propensity), and training reweights clicks by inverse propensity.
why: Click logs are the cheapest relevance signal for search and RAG rankers, but training on them raw just teaches the model to repeat its old ranking.
keyIdeas: Position bias: higher-ranked results get more clicks regardless of relevance, so raw clicks are biased labels
Position-based model: a click requires the result to be examined, and examination depends only on rank
Inverse propensity scoring gives an unbiased empirical risk estimate, even when queries do not repeat
Propensities can be estimated with small swap interventions instead of fully randomized rankings

name: Conversational query refinement (multi-turn state)
summary: Turning a context-dependent follow-up (with pronouns, ellipsis) into a self-contained query using the conversation history, so a standard retriever can answer each turn.
why: Chat-style RAG fails on follow-ups like 'what about its pricing?' unless the query is rewritten with the dialogue state before retrieval.
keyIdeas: Question-in-context rewriting: rewrite to a standalone question with the same answer (CANARD, 40,527 questions from QuAC)
TREC CAsT 2019 found a 35% relative gain for manually resolved utterances over the best automatic system
Condense-question pattern: an LLM rewrites history plus last message into one query, then retrieval runs on it
Tradeoff: always rewriting and retrieving handles knowledge questions but struggles with meta questions about the chat

name: Product quantization (PQ)
examples: Faiss IndexIVFPQ (IVFADC: coarse quantizer plus PQ on residuals)
summary: A vector compression method that splits each vector into M sub-vectors and quantizes each with its own k-means codebook, storing only the M centroid ids as a compact code.
why: Lets billion-scale embedding indexes fit in RAM or GPU memory and be searched fast, trading some recall for large memory savings.
keyIdeas: Code size is M times log2(K) bits, while the number of representable vectors is K to the power M
Search compares the query to codes in the compressed domain using per-query lookup tables
Often combined with an inverted file (IVF) so only a few partitions are scanned, with PQ encoding residuals
Knobs: more sub-vectors or bits per code improve accuracy at the cost of memory

name: Matryoshka embeddings (truncatable vectors)
summary: Embeddings trained so that prefixes of the vector (e.g. the first 64 or 256 dims) are themselves useful embeddings, letting one model serve multiple sizes by truncation.
why: Cuts vector storage and search cost in RAG systems without retraining, and enables cheap shortlist then full-size rerank pipelines.
keyIdeas: Training applies the same loss on several truncated prefixes (e.g. 768, 512, 256, 128, 64) and sums them
Adds no inference cost: just keep the first d dimensions at query and index time
MRL paper reports up to 14x smaller embeddings at equal ImageNet-1K accuracy
Two-stage use: shortlist with small vectors, then rerank the survivors with full-size vectors

name: Recommender systems and cold start
examples: Matrix factorization trained with SGD or WALS
summary: Systems that predict which items a user wants, typically by learning user and item embeddings from interaction data; cold start is the failure to recommend users or items with no training interactions.
why: The same retrieve, score, rerank stack and embedding tricks power LLM-era feeds, search and RAG ranking, and new items arrive constantly.
keyIdeas: Matrix factorization: predicted affinity is the dot product of a user embedding and an item embedding
Cold start: an item unseen in training has no embedding, so the model cannot score it
Mitigations: project a new item with a WALS step from a few interactions, or average embeddings of similar items
Wide & Deep combines a wide linear model (memorization) with a deep network (generalization)

links.label: Google ML: collaborative filtering pros and cons
Wide & Deep Learning for Recommender Systems (arXiv)

name: Constraint satisfaction solvers (CP and SAT)
summary: Constraint programming finds feasible assignments for variables with finite domains that satisfy every declared constraint, optionally optimizing an objective. You declare the rules; the solver searches.
why: Scheduling, allocation and packing problems explode combinatorially; a declarative model plus a solver beats hand-written search and is easy to extend with new rules.
keyIdeas: Model = integer or boolean variables + constraints (+ optional objective); CP focuses on feasibility rather than optimization
CP-SAT works over integers only: scale fractional coefficients up to integers before modelling
Global constraints capture common structure: add_all_different, interval variables with no_overlap and cumulative
Results report a status (OPTIMAL, FEASIBLE, INFEASIBLE, UNKNOWN); set max_time_in_seconds to bound search time

name: Metric learning and re-identification
summary: Metric learning trains a network to map inputs to embeddings where distance reflects identity, so the same person or object seen in different images lands close together. Re-identification then becomes nearest-neighbor search.
why: Matching the same entity across cameras or over time needs an embedding space where identity, not appearance noise, drives distance; the same idea underlies retrieval embeddings.
keyIdeas: Triplet loss: pull an anchor toward a same-label positive and push a different-label negative away by at least a margin m
Most random triplets are trivial, so mining matters: batch hard samples P identities x K images and uses the hardest pairs
No fixed class head: new identities at test time are handled by comparing embeddings, e.g. ranking a gallery per query
FaceNet reported 128-byte face embeddings usable directly for verification, recognition and clustering

links.label: In Defense of the Triplet Loss for ReID (arXiv)

name: Local feature matching (SIFT, ORB)
summary: Detect distinctive keypoints in each image, describe the patch around each with a descriptor vector, then pair descriptors across images by nearest-neighbor distance to find corresponding points.
why: Correspondences between images are the input to alignment, stitching, object finding and tracking, with no training data required.
keyIdeas: SIFT: DoG extrema across scale, orientation assignment, 128-value descriptor (patent expired 2020; now in main OpenCV)
ORB: FAST keypoints + rotation-steered BRIEF binary descriptor; much cheaper than SIFT, a fit for low-power devices
Match float descriptors with L2 and binary ones with Hamming distance; FLANN is faster than brute force on large sets
Filter ambiguous matches with Lowe's ratio test (best < 0.7 to 0.8 x second best; OpenCV uses 0.75) or cross-checking

name: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
summary: Estimate the geometric transform that maps one image onto another (a 3x3 homography for planar scenes or pure camera rotation), warp one into the other's frame, then compare aligned pixels to find what changed.
why: Before-and-after comparison only works once images line up pixel to pixel; otherwise every small camera shift shows up as a false change.
keyIdeas: A homography has 8 degrees of freedom and needs at least 4 point correspondences, usually from feature matching
RANSAC rejects bad matches as outliers; findHomography returns the inlier mask alongside the matrix
For pure translation, phase cross-correlation in Fourier space gives the shift with subpixel precision
After alignment, diff or SSIM the images; SSIM accounts for structure, so it tracks perceived change better than MSE

name: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
summary: Plate solving identifies where an image of the sky points by turning small groups of stars into shape codes that ignore position, rotation and scale, then looking those codes up in an index built from a star catalog.
why: It is a clean example of invariant hashing plus nearest-neighbor lookup plus hypothesis verification, the same retrieve-then-verify pattern used in large-scale search.
keyIdeas: Astrometry.net quad code: the widest pair A, B sets a local frame; C and D positions there form a 4-D hash vector
Codes are invariant to translation, rotation and scale; noise means lookup is a neighborhood search (kd-tree), not an exact key match
Each matching code is a hypothesis about pointing, scale and orientation, accepted only after a Bayesian verification test
astroalign matches 3-star triangles to estimate a similarity transform when corner features fail on point-like stars

name: Measuring size from a reference marker
summary: Put an object of known physical size (a printed fiducial marker, a coin, a card) in the same plane as the thing you want to measure; its known size converts pixel distances into real units.
why: Turns a single uncalibrated photo into real-world measurements, a common requirement for apps that estimate sizes, areas or distances from a phone camera.
keyIdeas: Scale = known marker width / marker width in pixels; only valid for objects in the marker's plane
A square marker's 4 corners give a homography to rectify the plane, removing perspective before measuring
ArUco markers carry a binary ID with error correction; pose from solvePnP is in the units of the marker side length
Lens distortion bends straight lines; calibrate once per camera (camera matrix + distortion coefficients) and undistort

name: LLM prompting and structured output
examples: OpenAI Structured Outputs (JSON Schema via response format or function calling)
summary: Techniques for steering an LLM with instructions and examples, and for forcing its output to match a format such as a JSON Schema, regex or grammar so downstream code can parse it reliably.
why: Agents, extractors and tool-calling pipelines break on malformed output; schema-constrained decoding turns free text into a dependable API contract.
keyIdeas: Chain-of-thought: a few exemplars with intermediate reasoning steps improve arithmetic and symbolic reasoning in large models
JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON; OpenAI Structured Outputs also guarantees adherence to your supplied JSON Schema
Guided generation compiles a regex or CFG into a finite-state machine and indexes the vocabulary to mask invalid tokens
Constraining at decode time beats parse-and-retry: little per-token overhead and far fewer outputs to repair (truncation still possible)

name: Anomaly and outlier detection
summary: Deciding whether an observation comes from the same distribution as the rest of the data. Outlier detection fits on contaminated data (unsupervised); novelty detection fits on clean data and flags new points (semi-supervised).
why: Flags bad sensor readings, data-pipeline corruption and odd traffic or metrics before they poison training data or dashboards.
keyIdeas: Isolation Forest: random feature and split value; anomalies are isolated in shorter average tree paths
Outlier methods assume anomalies sit in low-density regions and cannot form a dense cluster
scikit-learn thresholds a raw score_samples score; the contamination parameter sets the expected outlier fraction
OneClassSVM is sensitive to outliers; EllipticEnvelope assumes Gaussian data and fits an ellipse

name: Energy disaggregation (NILM)
examples: NILMTK: dataset converters, meters, preprocessing and metrics
Public datasets such as REDD, UK-DALE and REFIT
summary: Non-intrusive load monitoring separates a household's total energy use, measured at a single point such as a smart meter, into estimated per-appliance consumption.
why: A classic single-channel source separation problem on time series: a compact testbed for sequence models, benchmarks and reproducible evaluation.
keyIdeas: Input is one aggregate signal; output is appliance-level estimates, so it is an ill-posed inverse problem
Comparison was historically hard due to different datasets, missing reference implementations and varied metrics
NILMTK standardizes datasets (converted to HDF5), preprocessing, reference algorithms and accuracy metrics

name: Signal processing basics (filtering, FFT)
summary: Core tools for sampled time-domain signals: the discrete Fourier transform (computed via the FFT) maps a signal to its frequency spectrum, and digital filters remove noise or isolate frequency bands.
why: Sensor, audio and telemetry features (spectra, filtered signals, peaks) are standard preprocessing before any model sees the data.
keyIdeas: FFT computes the DFT fast; Cooley and Tukey brought it to light in its current form
For real input the spectrum is Hermitian, so rfft computes only non-negative frequencies
Forward-backward filtering (filtfilt, sosfiltfilt) gives zero phase; prefer SOS over [b, a] to avoid numerical problems
Downsample with an anti-aliasing filter first (decimate); Welch's method gives a smoothed PSD estimate

name: Spatial interpolation (IDW, kriging)
examples: GDAL gdal_grid inverse distance to a power
summary: Estimating values at unsampled locations from scattered point measurements, e.g. turning sensor readings into a grid. IDW uses distance weights; kriging derives weights from a fitted variogram or covariance model.
why: Turns sparse, irregular sensor or station data into dense maps and model features, with kriging adding a principled spatial correlation model.
keyIdeas: IDW: weighted average with weights 1/r^p, so a larger power p makes nearby points dominate
Kriging fits a variogram model (spherical, exponential, gaussian, etc.) then solves for weights
Ordinary kriging forces weights to sum to 1 (mean estimated); simple kriging needs a known mean
Universal kriging adds drift terms for trends; a nugget term models measurement error

name: Transit feeds (GTFS and GTFS-realtime)
examples: GTFS Schedule zip: stops.txt, routes.txt, trips.txt, stop_times.txt, calendar.txt
GTFS-realtime TripUpdate, VehiclePosition and Alert entities
summary: GTFS Schedule is a zip of text tables describing an agency's static timetable; GTFS-realtime is a Protocol Buffers feed of live updates (trip delays, vehicle positions, service alerts) keyed to it.
why: The standard input for transit ETA prediction, delay analytics and trip planners; joining live updates to static schedules is the core data task.
keyIdeas: Started as a TriMet (Portland) and Google collaboration, originally the Google Transit Feed Specification
A trip is a sequence of two or more stops; stop_times.txt holds per-stop arrival and departure times
Realtime FeedMessage holds FeedEntity items; StopTimeUpdate gives predicted times or a delay in seconds
GTFS-realtime is defined in proto2; delay is only meaningful relative to an existing GTFS schedule

name: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
examples: OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) on OpenStreetMap
summary: Finding the fastest or shortest route between points on a road network modeled as a weighted directed graph, typically built from OpenStreetMap with edge weights like length or travel time.
why: Underpins ETA, logistics and map-matching features; production engines rely on graph preprocessing to answer queries fast at scale.

OSRM keeps CH for special cases like very large distance matrices
OSRM and Valhalla also offer matrices and map matching of GPS traces to roads
